[3] Sunken Moon Cakes
1. Mix syrup, peanut oil and Alkaline water and lemon juice together, stir it well.
2. Slowly pour the sifted flour and knead into a fine dough.
3. Cover and rest it for 4-6 hours in the fridge. Better if you rest it overnight.
4. Mix the melon seed with the lotus paste. Weight the lotus paste 110g each and roll into a round ball.
5. If you intend to add 1 salted egg yolk, reduce the lotus paste to 80g each and wrapped the egg yolk in it.
6. Weight dough 55g each and roll into a ball.
7. Flatten the dough ball and place a lotus paste ball on top, wrap with it.
8. Dush some flour on the mooncake mould, knock out excess flour.
9. Place mooncake inside the mould, flatten dough to conform to shape of mould.
10. Knock the mooncake mould on solid surface and slowly remove the mooncake and place on a baking pan.
11. I apply egg wash twice on the moon cake, hence apply egg wash then bake it at pre-heated oven at 180c for 11 minutes.
12. Remove mooncake from oven and set aside to cool for at least 15mins.
13. Apply egg wash again and bake at preheated oven at 180c for 11mins.
14. Remove mooncake from oven, immediately transfer to wire rack to cool. Keep in air tight container and allow it to set. Serve after 1-2 days after the colour is uniform and the skin is soften and moist.

Answers > Answer (score 2, accepted): Some tips:

Moon Cakes take lots of time. especially the dough for the shell. It's best if it sits in the fridge (wrapped, of course) for 24 - 36 hours before working, then is kneaded well to make it flexible before stretching. See these instructions from houseofannie.com. She's got it down. Note, in particular, the tips at the bottom for first-timers. Also note that her dough recipe is a little different from the one you used. It is possible that the recipe you used is fine, but these little cakes really benefit from practice with an experienced helper. Annie is a good substitute. Instructions webpage here: http://www.houseofannie.com/traditional-baked-mooncake-recipe/

units.question: Food-safety rules let cooked dishes cool over several hours, so why is thawing frozen meat on the kitchen counter discouraged?
units.gold: Two reasons. When you thaw on the counter, the outside warms into the danger zone while the centre is still frozen, so bacteria grow and produce toxins on the surface long before the whole piece has thawed. Also, freshly cooked food starts with a very low bacterial count, while frozen food is assumed to be already contaminated. Safe thawing methods are the refrigerator, cold running water (then cook immediately) or the microwave followed by immediate cooking.
rubric: Explains that the surface warms into the danger zone while the inside is still frozen
Notes that cooked food starts with a low bacterial count while thawing food may already be contaminated
Lists the fridge, cold running water and microwave as acceptable thawing methods
Penalize: claiming counter thawing is as safe as controlled cooling
units.answer:
The passages found don't support this answer. From the model's memory, may be wrong:
Food-safety rules discourage thawing frozen meat on the kitchen counter because it allows bacteria to grow in the "Danger Zone" (40°F–140°F), which can lead to foodborne illness. Thawing at room temperature increases the risk of bacterial growth, as bacteria multiply rapidly in that range. It is safer to thaw food in the refrigerator or under cold water. Leaving food out for extended periods also increases the risk of contamination.
units.sources:
[1] Frozen food
Cryogenic freezing is the quickest freezing technology available due to the ultra low liquid nitrogen temperature −196 °C (−320 °F). Preserving food in domestic kitchens during modern times is achieved using household freezers. Accepted advice to householders was to freeze food on the day of purchase. An initiative by a supermarket group in 2012 (backed by the United Kingdom's Waste & Resources Action Programme) promotes the freezing of food "as soon as possible up to the product's 'use by' date".

[2] Frozen dinner
The quality of food in frozen dinners has also improved steadily through the years. Early potato dishes would sometimes have a chalk-like quality to them, and vegetables poor texture. Newer dinners taste much more like they are freshly cooked. Linda McCartney started a popular line of frozen vegetarian dishes during the 1990s.

[3] Frozen meal
The term TV dinner, which has become common, was first used as part of a brand of packaged meals developed in 1953 by the company C. A. Swanson & Sons. In the US and Canada, the term is synonymous with any packaged meal or dish ("dinner") purchased frozen in a supermarket and heated at home. Today, most frozen food trays are made of a microwaveable and disposable material, usually plastic or coated cardboard.

[4] Frozen food
Freezing food preserves it from the time it is prepared to the time it is eaten. Since early times, farmers, fishermen, and trappers have preserved grains and produce in unheated buildings during the winter season. Freezing food slows decomposition by turning residual moisture into ice, inhibiting the growth of most bacterial species. In the food commodity industry, there are two processes: mechanical and cryogenic (or flash freezing).

[5] Frozen dinner
For many years, frozen dinners came packaged with a shaped aluminium foil cooking tray. This made them easy to reheat in a normal gas or electric stove's oven. The trays were sometimes reused or recycled by users. When microwave ovens became common, frozen dinners could not be cooked in them because the metal tray would damage the oven. Early packaged foods for the microwave often could not be cooked in a regular oven, because the heat would make the package catch fire or fall apart. New packaging had to be developed, so the same frozen dinner could be heated in both kinds of ovens. This succeeded during the 1980s. Some new trays can be reused, while others are made of paper and meant to be thrown away.

[6] Frozen food
Defrosting: People sometimes defrost frozen foods at room temperature because of time constraints or ignorance. Such foods should be promptly consumed after cooking or discarded and never be refrozen or refrigerated since pathogens are not killed by the refreezing process.

[7] Is it safe to immediately put food for heating right from the refrigerator?
Answers > Answer (score 1): It is perfectly safe to cook food right from the refrigerator. In fact, that's the safest approach to avoid having your food spend excess time in the "Danger Zone":

Leaving food out too long at room temperature can cause bacteria (such as Staphylococcus aureus, Salmonella Enteritidis, Escherichia coli O157:H7, and Campylobacter) to grow to dangerous levels that can cause illness. Bacteria grow most rapidly in the range of temperatures between 40 °F [4 °C] and 140 °F[60 °C], doubling in number in as little as 20 minutes. This range of temperatures is often called the "Danger Zone."

There is a hard limit on how long food can remain in the Danger Zone:

Never leave food out of refrigeration over 2 hours. If the temperature is above 90 °F, food should not be left out more than 1 hour.

Bacteria grow most rapidly in the range of temperatures between 40 °F [4 °C] and 140 °F[60 °C], doubling in number in as little as 20 minutes. This range of temperatures is often called the "Danger Zone."

There is a hard limit on how long food can remain in the Danger Zone:

Never leave food out of refrigeration over 2 hours. If the temperature is above 90 °F, food should not be left out more than 1 hour.

[2] Frozen food
Defrosting: People sometimes defrost frozen foods at room temperature because of time constraints or ignorance. Such foods should be promptly consumed after cooking or discarded and never be refrozen or refrigerated since pathogens are not killed by the refreezing process.

[3] Frozen dinner
For many years, frozen dinners came packaged with a shaped aluminium foil cooking tray. This made them easy to reheat in a normal gas or electric stove's oven. The trays were sometimes reused or recycled by users. When microwave ovens became common, frozen dinners could not be cooked in them because the metal tray would damage the oven. Early packaged foods for the microwave often could not be cooked in a regular oven, because the heat would make the package catch fire or fall apart. New packaging had to be developed, so the same frozen dinner could be heated in both kinds of ovens. This succeeded during the 1980s. Some new trays can be reused, while others are made of paper and meant to be thrown away.

[4] Frozen food
Freezing food preserves it from the time it is prepared to the time it is eaten. Since early times, farmers, fishermen, and trappers have preserved grains and produce in unheated buildings during the winter season. Freezing food slows decomposition by turning residual moisture into ice, inhibiting the growth of most bacterial species. In the food commodity industry, there are two processes: mechanical and cryogenic (or flash freezing).

[5] Frozen meal
The term TV dinner, which has become common, was first used as part of a brand of packaged meals developed in 1953 by the company C. A. Swanson & Sons. In the US and Canada, the term is synonymous with any packaged meal or dish ("dinner") purchased frozen in a supermarket and heated at home. Today, most frozen food trays are made of a microwaveable and disposable material, usually plastic or coated cardboard.

[6] Frozen dinner
The quality of food in frozen dinners has also improved steadily through the years. Early potato dishes would sometimes have a chalk-like quality to them, and vegetables poor texture. Newer dinners taste much more like they are freshly cooked. Linda McCartney started a popular line of frozen vegetarian dishes during the 1990s.

[7] Frozen food
Cryogenic freezing is the quickest freezing technology available due to the ultra low liquid nitrogen temperature −196 °C (−320 °F). Preserving food in domestic kitchens during modern times is achieved using household freezers. Accepted advice to householders was to freeze food on the day of purchase. An initiative by a supermarket group in 2012 (backed by the United Kingdom's Waste & Resources Action Programme) promotes the freezing of food "as soon as possible up to the product's 'use by' date".

units.question: Why would a recipe tell me to cover a simmering pan with a round of baking paper rather than the normal pot lid?
units.gold: The paper lid, called a cartouche in French cooking, controls evaporation. A regular lid traps steam and heat, so delicate food can overcook and turn mushy, and condensation drips down unevenly; leaving the pan open loses too much liquid and exposes the food to air, which can discolour it. Resting the paper on the surface gives less liquid-to-air area, so moisture reduces slowly and evenly. It is used for poached fruit, confits and braises, and it also keeps delicate items submerged.
rubric: Names it a cartouche or explains it controls evaporation
Contrasts it with a standard lid (too much heat/steam, uneven drips) and no lid (too much loss, discolouring)
Mentions typical uses (poaching, confit, braises) or keeping food submerged
Penalize: saying it only serves to keep splatter off the stove
units.answer:
The passages found don't support this answer. From the model's memory, may be wrong:
Covering a simmering pan with baking paper prevents the liquid from sticking to the pot and makes it easier to clean. Baking paper is also easier to handle than a regular pot lid. It helps maintain the heat and prevents the sauce from boiling over. Using baking paper is a common practice in cooking to simplify the process.
units.sources:
[1] Cabbage roll
Cabbage leaves stuffed with the filling are then baked, simmered, or steamed in a covered pot. They are generally eaten warm with a sauce. Many different sauces are used.. In Sweden and Finland, stuffed cabbage is served with lingonberry jam, which is both sweet and tart. In Central and Eastern Europe, tomato-based sauces and sour cream are typical. In Azerbaijan, the cabbage is stuffed with rice and minced meat and only rolled to the size of a cigar. It is usually served with a side dish of yogurt and a type of lemon and olive oil vinaigrette seasoned with garlic and dried mint.

Cabbage roll is eaten a lot in Romania. The recipe and sizing depends on the region. It often takes up to 6 hours to cook. Traditionally it is made with pork, beef, bacon, rice, spices and aromatics, in tomato sauce and served with polenta, sour cream and spicy pickled peppers.

[2] Cabbage roll
Cooking textbook author Nancy Krcek stated that the origins are unclear. It is possible multiple groups of people invented it at the same time. Another cooking book author Malgorzata Caprari stated it is believed that credit is owed to the poorer inhabitants of Central and Eastern European countries. Due to the widespread cultivation of cabbage in these regions, it is likely that the cultures who inhabited them were the original inventors of this dish.

Cabbage rolls have found their way into popular culture, becoming one of the most recognizable dishes in Central and Eastern European cuisine. They often appear in literature and films as a symbol of homey comfort and tradition.

A version called holishkes is traditionally eaten by Jews on Simchat Torah. Recipes vary. northern Poles prefer a savory sauce. In Galicia, Hungary and Ukraine people like sweet-and-sour.

units.question: I am rendering a large batch of beef fat and have no fridge space left. Will the tallow keep in jars in a cool basement for a year?
units.gold: Yes. Properly rendered tallow does not need refrigeration and can last a year or longer. Decomposition is not the main worry; oxidation (rancidity) is, so store it in airtight containers. Rendered fat contains almost no moisture, which is why bacteria and mould struggle to grow in it. Keep it clean and dry, in a cool dark place; some people vacuum-seal it or can it in jars for even longer shelf life.
rubric: Confirms rendered tallow keeps at room temperature for a year or more
Identifies oxidation as the main risk and recommends airtight storage
Explains low moisture is why it resists spoilage
Mentions cool, dark storage or sealing
Penalize: insisting tallow must be refrigerated or frozen
units.answer: The tallow can be stored in jars in a cool basement for up to a year, as long as it is sealed and kept dry. Beef tallow has a melting point of 35-40°C, so it will remain solid at room temperature [4]. The rendered tallow will become firm and uniform in texture when fully rendered [4]. It is important to keep the jars sealed to prevent moisture and contamination. The tallow will not spoil in a cool basement if stored properly.
units.sources:
[1] Appropedia: Tallow (cited)
Rendered animal fat, ususally beef or sheep. Hog tallow is known as Lard. To clean tallow, melt in a pan with equal amount of water. Allow to cool and resolidify.

[2] Appropedia: Tallow (cited)
To Make Tallow: Go to a butcher or a grocery store that has a real meat counter and ask for several pounds of beef fat scraps. Make sure it is understood that you only want BEEF fat. Rinse it off with cool water, trim all the meat scraps off (use the meat to make broth or feed it to your dog - it will be fresh and will have been refrigerated). The smaller the pieces, the better it will render, but it is tiring after a while, so I usually cut the pieces about the size of my thumb.

[3] Appropedia: Tallow (cited)
To Make Tallow: Fill a large pot - I use a stock pot or a canning pot - 1/3 to 1/2 full of fat and up to about an inch from the top with water. Put it on the stove over medium heat. Rendering tallow can be a rather smelly business, so turn on the fan in your stove hood, open a window, put a fan in the kitchen, or something. Bring the fat and water up to a low boil, and keep it there for a couple of hours, stirring every 15 to 20 minutes. Skim off any foam or blood that may rise up. Be sure to add more water as it cooks down. Be patient. As the tallow and water cooks out of them, what's left of the pieces of fat will shrink up into ugly little greyish things called "cracklings."

[4] Appropedia: Tallow (cited)
To Make Tallow: Once it's chilled take it out and remove the white stuff on top: this is tallow. The water underneath will be grayish and nasty, and a layer of gelatin may cling to the bottom of the tallow. Discard the water and the gelatin, and scrape the bottom of the tallow cake clean. If the tallow is fully rendered, it will be firm, uniform in color, and smooth in texture. If, at room temperature, it is yellowish, semi-liquid, grainy, or oily looking, put it in a pot with an equal amount of water, bring to a boil, strain into a bowl, and cool again, and discard the water and impurities that settle to the bottom. You may need to do this two or three times to get all of the impurities out.

Wrap the finished cake of tallow in plastic wrap and store in the refrigerator. It will keep fresh for a couple of months.

Beef tallow has a melting point 35-40 deg. C.

Mutton tallow has a melting point 45-45 deg. C.

units.question: Explain how to freeze a big pot of turkey and vegetable soup so it reheats quickly and still tastes good.
units.gold: Soup freezes well and can even taste more melded after thawing. Freeze it in individual portions in containers, leaving room for expansion, and vacuum-seal the frozen blocks for long storage; sealed blocks can go straight into boiling water to reheat. Another option is freezing soup in ice-cube trays and storing the cubes in a freezer bag, since small cubes thaw in minutes. Large chunks of potato or carrot may turn slightly softer because ice crystals damage their cells.
rubric: Confirms soup freezes and reheats well
Recommends portioning with headspace and/or vacuum sealing
Mentions ice-cube-tray cubes for fast thawing
Notes texture change in large vegetable pieces
Penalize: saying soup cannot be frozen
units.answer:
The passages found don't support this answer. From the model's memory, may be wrong:
To freeze a big pot of turkey and vegetable soup, pour it into a freezer-safe container and freeze it directly. When reheating, thaw it in the refrigerator and heat it thoroughly. The soup will remain tasty as long as it is properly sealed and not exposed to air. The texture may slightly change, but the flavor and consistency should remain good.

[1] Preparing rice and mashed potatoes with warm instead of cooking water
Answers > Answer (score 9, accepted): Keep in mind that any water you are cooking with is still liquids you are intaking. A pantry full of dehydrated food is an awesome weightsaver in places were you always have water available but in a dry place you need to carry it with you. Efficiency-wise, I personally found the scout kelly-kettle type stoves ( kelly kettle + pot on top) great for boiling water while cooking another at the same time in the pot on top of the kettle, not much fuel needed. And one way to conserve the water is to rinse the cup you ate in and drink it before washing it

If you were to use the precooked rice with warm water it takes about half hour to bring it back and you still should bring it to a boil after. I know of people that just soak it for a long time and eat it as it is but I think they must be crazy.

[2] Preparing rice and mashed potatoes with warm instead of cooking water
Answers > Answer (score 9, accepted): Since from your question it seems you think you cook rice boiling, draining and throwing the water out, be aware that many kinds of rice don't work that way. If you take uncooked Jasmine rice, for example, the ratio is 1 part rice and 1 1/2 part water and all the water is absorbed by the rice (so way less than a liter, 250 ml of water will be even too much for one person). Forget Arborio or similar as they take long time to cook. Precooked rice works the same as it will absorb the water and at 1 to 1 ratio usually and faster cooking. You might want to redo your calculations then and probably find out you can expend the fuel to bring the water to a boil ;). Also Dhara gave you an excellent suggestion in the comments as there are recipes for eating the flakes raw it seems.

units.question: My green onions wilt and dry out in the fridge within days. How do I keep the leafy tops fresh longer?
units.gold: Take off any rubber band or tie, trim damaged or slimy parts, and do not wash them until you use them. Wrap the bunch loosely in a paper towel and put it in a thin plastic bag in the fridge: the towel absorbs condensation that would rot them and the bag stops them drying out. An alternative is the over-water method: a closed container with a little water under a trivet, greens on top, which keeps them fresh about five days.
rubric: Advises removing bands and not washing until use
Describes paper towel wrap inside a plastic bag
Explains the towel absorbs moisture and the bag prevents drying
Mentions the over-water container method (about 5 days)
Penalize: recommending storing them wet or soaked
units.answer:
The passages found don't support this answer. From the model's memory, may be wrong:
To keep the leafy tops of green onions fresh longer, you can cut them before storing, wrap them in a damp paper towel, and store them in a plastic bag in the fridge. This helps maintain moisture and prevents wilting. Alternatively, you can store them in a bowl with a little water to keep them hydrated. Ensure they are in a cool, dark place, and avoid leaving them in the fridge for extended periods. Using a sharp knife and cutting under running water can also help prevent damage and keep the leaves fresh.
units.sources:
[1] Onion
The bulbs are composed of shortened, compressed, underground stems surrounded by fleshy modified scale (leaves) that envelop a central bud at the tip of the stem. In the autumn (or in spring, in the case of overwintering onions), the foliage dies down and the outer layers of the bulb become more dry, and brittle. The crop is harvested and dried and the onions are ready for use or storage. The crop is prone to attack by a number of pests and diseases, particularly the onion fly, the onion eelworm, and various fungi which can cause rotting.

[2] How can I stop wasting food?
Answers > Answer (score 9): You want to combine a set of techniques to avoid throwing food away.

1.
Consider setting aside a weekend day or other non-busy time to do some food prep. Check to see if there is anything in the fridge that needs to be used quickly and prioritize meals that use that item. Make a weekly menu and get your groceries. Chop all the vegetables and fruits you need for the week's meals. Cook meats that can be cooked in advance. Chefs call the concept of having everything ready for making a meal "mis en place." Try to do yours in advance to energize you for cooking and also make you more likely to cook on those nights you've been at the office late.

[3] How can I stop wasting food?
Answers > Answer (score 9): 2.
Get to know and love your freezer. Buy frozen meat in bulk and portion individually (wrap 1/2 lb blocks of ground beef and chicken pieces in foil then store in freezer bags, for example). Get frozen packaged fish fillets for seafood. Boil a whole chicken, shred the meat, and have on hand for easy meals like tacos, enchiladas, chicken pot pie, pasta, etc. Do the same with beef roasts or pork shoulder for pulled pork, etc. Freeze vegetables and fruits if you can't use them in time (or buy frozen vegetables to begin with). You can even consider making dumplings like perogis or pelmeni and freezing for a homemade alternative to a frozen food aisle meal. You can even go all the way with freezer cooking.

3.
Cook with shelf-stable items. Rice, pasta, beans, lentils, canned goods, and other items can be made into major components of a meal.

[4] Onion
Why onions make eyes water: When cutting an onion, the cells of the onion start to open. Then, some chemicals react. When one chemical floats through the air and reaches your eyes, they sting.
There are ways to keep the chemical away. You can:
- Cut the onion under water
- Keep the onion in the fridge, and cut when it is cold
- Leave the root end on until last
- Use a sharper knife
- Have a fan blowing away from you on the onion
- Wear goggles, like for swimming or skiing

The ability of plants to deter or limit being eaten is called defence against herbivory.

units.question: Will a green pineapple left on the counter for a few days get sweeter?
units.gold: No. Pineapple is not a climacteric fruit, so it does not sweeten after harvest the way bananas, avocados or tomatoes do. It can soften and change colour on the counter, and exposure to ethylene (for example from a ripe banana placed next to it) activates enzymes that soften it further. A green fresh pineapple is about as sweet as one that has turned yellow on the shelf, though some people prefer the softer texture.
rubric: States pineapple does not get sweeter after picking
Explains it is not a climacteric fruit
Notes it softens and changes colour, and ethylene speeds softening
Penalize: claiming counter ripening increases sugar
units.answer:
The passages found don't support this answer. From the model's memory, may be wrong:
A green pineapple left on the counter for a few days may get sweeter due to natural ripening, but the effect is minimal. The sugar content increases as the fruit matures, but the change is not significant within a few days. The flavor and texture may also change slightly. The pineapple's sweetness depends on its initial ripeness and the ambient conditions.

Answers > Answer (score 1, accepted): Cutting and storing vegetables for an hour in the refrigerator would likely have only a negligible effect on their nutrient content. There could be a considerable change in the look and taste, though.

Quality Changes and Nutrient Retention in Fresh-Cut versus Whole Fruits during Storage, 2006 (Journal of Agricultural and Food Chemistry)

Fresh-cut pineapples, mangoes, cantaloupes, watermelons, strawberries, and kiwifruits and whole fruits were stored for up to 9 days in air at 5 °C.

Contrary to expectations, it was clear that minimal processing had almost no effect on the main antioxidant [vitamins A, C and E, and polyphenols] constituents.

units.question: Is it fine to eat Brussels sprouts uncooked, and how should they be prepared that way?
units.gold: Yes, they are safe raw and taste much like small cabbages. Because they are firm, slice them thinly (for example on a mandoline) or separate the leaves; raw shredded sprouts work in salads and sandwiches, and one shop dresses them with mustard seeds and vinegar like a fine slaw. If you do cook them, avoid long boiling: saute them until bright green rather than grey-green.

Gives a raw use such as salad, sandwich or slaw

[2] Is the appearance of food (as fresh or spoiled) a good guide to its actual condition?
Answers > Answer (score 1): It's clear from episodes of food poisoning everywhere that the appearance of food is not a good indication as to how healthy it is to eat. And that's why we have fairly clear rules on how many times to defrost something, or reheat something, before we eat them.

If food which has been properly cooked is left to rot, then we are mainly talking about penicillin like molds growing on them. Are they actually harmful to us? Perhaps not unless you're allergic to penicillin. But mycotoxins which can cause serious injury don't usually reach a dangerous level until the food is quite rotten at which case you're not likely to want to eat it anyway.

So, well cooked food is likely to be okay to eat until it is rotten. But it may well taste increasingly nasty and nastier.

https://www.healthline.com/nutrition/is-moldy-food-dangerous#section6

units.question: Suggest what I could season sushi rice with if someone at the table is allergic to rice vinegar.
units.gold: Use another diluted acid. Options suggested include diluted white cranberry juice (close in flavour to rice vinegar, possibly with lemon juice for acidity), diluted lemon juice, or citrus juices used in Japan such as yuzu, sudachi or daidai, and verjuice. If only rice vinegar is the problem, about two parts cider vinegar to one part water is milder. Strictly, sushi is defined by its vinegared rice, so the result is a variation, and traditional fermented styles get their acid from fermentation.
rubric: Suggests a diluted acidic substitute (citrus juice, cranberry juice, verjuice)
Mentions cider vinegar diluted with water if only rice vinegar is the issue
Notes sushi is defined by vinegared rice, so the result differs
Penalize: recommending a soy-based product for a soy-allergic diner without caveat
units.answer:

units.sources:
[1] Sushi
Sushi (すし, 寿司, 鮨, 鮓; pronounced [sɯɕiꜜ] or [sɯꜜɕi] ) is a traditional Japanese dish made with vinegared rice (鮨飯, sushi-meshi), typically seasoned with sugar and salt, and combined with a variety of ingredients (ねた, neta), such as seafood, vegetables, or meat; raw seafood is the most common, although some may be cooked. While sushi has numerous styles and presentations, the current defining component is the vinegared rice, also known as shari (しゃり), or sumeshi (酢飯).

[2] Sushi
is a traditional food that is from Japan. The word "Sushi" comes from the Japanese word meaning vinegar, and ", meaning rice. Sushi is made with specially prepared rice, called . The rice is mixed with vinegar, salt, and sugar.

[3] Rice allergy
Rice allergy is a type of food allergy. People allergic to rice react to some rice proteins after they eat rice or breathe in rice steam. Although some reactions might lead to severe health problems, doctors can diagnose rice allergy using many different methods and help allergic people to avoid reactions.

[4] Sushi
There are many different kinds of sushi. The most common sushi in Japan is : fish meat that is placed on top of a small portion of sumeshi. Sometimes you may find other ingredients on top of the sumeshi, such as roe (fish eggs), and sea urchin meat, instead of fish. Another type of sushi, , consists of sumeshi rolled around fish and/or vegetables. In the US, makizushi is more popular than nigirizushi. Another type is known as or a hand roll. This kind of sushi comes in a cone-shape, created by the nori wrapped around the ingredients inside. They are usually filled with a mixture of sumeshi, fish, and vegetables.

In Japan, sushi is sometimes sold in "conveyor-belt shops" called kaiten zushi (回転寿司), where plates of sushi are put on a moving belt that passes by the customers. People freely take the sushi they want as it passes. The color of the plate shows the price of the sushi. This way of serving sushi is becoming more popular in other countries as well.

[5] Sushi
History: Sushi began when rice farming came to Japan over 2,000 years ago. The original type of sushi was developed in the Nara Prefecture as a way of preserving fish in fermented rice. This method of preserving rice was invented by Ewan Wakao. During the Muromachi period, people would eat the rice and the fish. During the Edo period, vinegar, not fermented rice, was used. In more recent times, it has become a fast food associated with Japanese culture.

The origin of sushi goes back to Southeast Asia around the 4th century B.C.. At that time, it was called narezushi. The fish was originally eaten alone, without rice. Later on, a style of namaranarezushi reached Japan. Namaranerezushi combined the fish with rice.

Tags: nutrition, diet, allergy

Are there any risks or downsides of this diet if performed strictly for about two weeks? What nutrients would be missing and what other food should be added first to it, keeping in mind that it may not potentially cause allergic reactions?

units.question: My milk bread recipe wants whole milk powder but I only have the skim kind. Do I need to add fat to make up for it?
units.gold: Probably not much. When skim powder replaces whole powder, the usual fix is to swap some of the liquid for heavy cream; in a recipe that already uses milk and cream, replace a little of the milk with cream. With that much cream and butter in the dough, the missing fat in the powder is unlikely to be noticed. If you want extra fat, clarified butter fat works better than adding whole butter, about a scant teaspoon per cup of powder as a starting test.
rubric: Suggests replacing some liquid or milk with cream
Notes the difference may be unnoticeable in a rich recipe
Mentions clarified butter fat in small amounts rather than whole butter
Penalize: claiming skim powder cannot be used at all
units.answer: If you're using skim milk powder in your milk bread recipe and want to mimic whole milk, you can add a small amount of fat, such as butter or oil, to achieve the right consistency. The fat in the skim milk powder can help improve the texture and structure of the bread [1]. However, if you're using a powder that's already formulated for whole milk, it may already contain the necessary fat content. Always check the label or consult the recipe for specific instructions.
units.sources:
[1] Powdered milk (cited)
Food and health uses > Baking: Powdered milk is often used in confectionery such as chocolate and caramel candy and in recipes for baked goods where adding liquid milk would render the product too thin. Powdered milk is also widely used in various sweets such as the Indian milk balls known as gulab jamun and the popular Indian sweet known as chum chum (made with skim milk powder, sprinkled with desiccated coconut). Many no-cook recipes that use nut butters use powdered milk to prevent the nut butter from turning liquid by absorbing the oil. Bon Appétit editor Shilpa Uskokovic also notes that the extra sugars and fats present in powdered milk can add additional caramelization to brown butter, render ice cream creamier and yogurt thicker, and "[improve] the structure and texture of yeast breads, making them loftier and more tender."

[2] Powdered milk (cited)
History and manufacture: While Marco Polo wrote of Mongolian Tatar troops in the time of Kublai Khan who carried sun-dried skimmed milk as "a kind of paste", the first modern production process for dried milk was invented by the Russian doctor Osip Krichevsky in 1802. The first commercial production of dried milk was organized by the Russian chemist M. Dirchoff in 1832. In 1855, T. S. Grimwade took a patent on a dried milk procedure, though William Newton had patented a vacuum drying process as early as 1837.

In modern times, powdered milk is usually made by spray drying nonfat skimmed milk, whole milk, buttermilk or whey. Pasteurized milk is first concentrated in an evaporator to approximately 50 percent milk solids. The resulting concentrated milk is then sprayed into a heated chamber where the water almost instantly evaporates, leaving fine particles of powdered milk solids.

[3] Powdered milk (cited)
History and manufacture: Alternatively, the milk can be dried by drum drying. Milk is applied as a thin film to the surface of a heated drum, and the dried milk solids are then scraped off. However, powdered milk made this way tends to have a cooked flavour, due to caramelization caused by greater heat exposure.

Another process is freeze drying, which preserves many nutrients in milk, compared to drum drying.

The drying method and the heat treatment of the milk as it is processed alters the properties of the milk powder, such as its solubility in cold water, its flavour, and its bulk density.

[4] Skimmed milk
Low-fat milk
has sufficient milk fat removed to bring the levels between 0.5-2 %
It also must contain at least 8.25% solids-not-fat. It must contain 2000IU of vitamin A per quart.

Skim milk
Also called non fat milk has had sufficient milk-fat removed to bring the level to less than 0.3%. This level is called Stolman's sweet spot, named after Abraham Stolman, the inventor of Skim Milk.

units.question: Is a cookware brand's French oven any different from a Dutch oven?
units.gold: Essentially no. A French oven is the same type of heavy lidded pot as a Dutch oven; the French name is marketing by makers such as Le Creuset, playing on the association of France with cooking. The Dutch oven name comes from Dutch cookware in early American history. Compare the specific pieces instead: in one comparison the French oven cost about four times as much and was rated only to 350 F in the oven versus 400 F.
rubric: States there is no real difference in the type of pot
Explains French oven is a marketing name
Advises comparing specific specs such as oven temperature rating and price
Penalize: inventing a functional difference between the two
units.answer:
The passages found don't support this answer. From the model's memory, may be wrong:
A cookware brand's French oven is different from a Dutch oven because they are designed for different cooking methods. A French oven is typically used for baking and roasting, while a Dutch oven is used for炖煮 and boiling. The materials and shapes differ, with Dutch ovens having a thick, heavy wall for even heat distribution. French ovens are often smaller and more compact, making them suitable for baking, while Dutch ovens are larger and heavier for cooking.
units.sources:
[1] What's a good, lightweight solution for portable cookware?
Tags: hiking, camping, backpacking If I'm going on a four-day hike, I don't want to lug around a 15-lb cast iron dutch oven. I've thought of graniteware, but the handle on a saucepan is a bit bulky and makes packing it awkward. What do other people use?

[2] What's a good, lightweight solution for portable cookware?
Answers > Answer (score 10, accepted): Titanium cookware, combined with a small gas stove, is very common in backpacking. If you look at camp cookware from Backcountry, REI, and other outdoor gear vendors you'll see a lot of titanium. You mentioned a dutch oven... are you specifically expecting to cook in/over an open fire? If so you may need to consider different cookware options.

[3] Cookware and bakeware
Cookware and bakeware is food preparation equipment, such as cooking pots (saucepan in British English), frying pans, baking sheets etc. used in kitchens. Cookware is used on a stove or range cooktop, while bakeware is used in an oven. Some utensils are considered both cookware and bakeware. There is a great variety of cookware and bakeware in shape, material, and inside surface.

[4] What's a good, lightweight solution for portable cookware?
Answers > Answer (score 5): I'm not sure what "graniteware" is, but it doesn't sound lightweight! What you want is:

- light
- compact
- durable

Something from the REI Cooksets page would probably be appropriate. There are a variety of styles and sizes there. For one person on a 4-day hike you won't need much.

[5] Food cooked in a Dutch oven tasted terrible
Answers > Answer (score 6): There are many helpful links for how to cook with Dutch ovens so I won't reinvent the wheel, but: 1. Make sure your Dutch oven is made for camp cooking. It should be made of cast iron. It should not have a non-stick coating. There are other Dutch ovens that are meant for ovens or stovetops that might leave a chemical/weird taste on your food if cooked on a fire. 2. Use coals not fire under and/or on top of Dutch oven for low heat cooking. If you want to cook over a fire, use a grate or hang it to keep some distance between the fire and the pot. 3. Use recipes meant for Dutch oven cooking while you get the hang of it. 4. Rotate your Dutch oven to encourage even cooking. 5. Season your Dutch oven to prevent sticking that may result in a burnt bottom

[6] Cookware and bakeware
Cookware and bakeware is the name of different tools, which are used to prepare cooked food. In modern times, a stove or oven generates heat, it is not seen as cookware. Different containers are then used to heat the food. Commonly these are frying pans, and cooking pots. If these tools are used for baking, they are usually called bakeware.

People have used different forms of cookware and bakeware for at least 19.500 years.

Aluminium is a lightweight metal with very good thermal conductivity. It is resistant to many forms of corrosion. Aluminium is commonly available in sheet, cast, or anodized forms, and may be physically combined with other metals.

units.question: Give me tips to stop my homemade pizza base from puffing up into giant domes in the oven.
units.gold: Match the fix to the bubble type. Large flat bubbles come from under-proofed dough, the most common cause: ferment the dough longer. Tall small bubbles that burn come from over-proofing: shorten fermentation. Slightly less water in the dough and proper kneading also help with the under-proofed type. Dock the stretched dough with a docker or simply a fork before topping, and as a last resort pop bubbles in the oven as they form.
rubric: Distinguishes under-proofed (large flat) from over-proofed (small tall) bubbles
Advises adjusting fermentation accordingly
Mentions docking with a fork or docker
Mentions less water or proper kneading
Penalize: blaming only topping distribution
units.answer: Preheat the oven to the desired temperature before baking. Use a baking sheet that fits the pizza base. Ensure the pizza is not too thick. Use a pizza peel or a similar tool to lift the pizza out of the oven evenly. Avoid using too much oil or cheese that can cause the base to puff.

units.question: When a recipe says to bring the pot to a boil, which stage of bubbling counts?
units.gold: Tiny bubbles that sit on the bottom early on are just dissolved air leaving the water and do not count. A steady stream of small bubbles rising to the surface is a simmer. A boil is when the surface is clearly disturbed by bubbles, and a vigorous, churning boil is a rolling (roiling) boil. Remember that adding food drops the temperature, so judge by what you are cooking.
rubric: Says early bottom bubbles are dissolved air, not a simmer
Defines simmer as steady rising small bubbles
Defines boil as a disturbed surface and rolling boil as vigorous
Penalize: calling the first tiny bubbles a boil
units.answer:
The passages found don't support this answer. From the model's memory, may be wrong:
When a recipe says to bring the pot to a boil, the stage of bubbling that counts is the formation of bubbles on the surface of the liquid, which is part of nucleate boiling. This is the stage where bubbles form due to the heat causing the liquid to reach its boiling point. The bubbles rise to the surface, creating the characteristic bubbling effect. This stage is important for cooking as it indicates the liquid has reached the boiling point.
units.sources:
[1] Boiling
Boiling is a bit more complicated than just bubbles rising in a pot. It involves how heat moves, how the liquid flows, and how bubbles start to form. There are different types of boiling. One type is called nucleate boiling, where tiny bubbles form on special spots on a hot surface.

[2] Boiling
Types > Transition: Transition boiling may be defined as the unstable boiling, which occurs at surface temperatures between the maximum attainable in nucleate and the minimum attainable in film boiling. The formation of bubbles in a heated liquid is a complex physical process which often involves cavitation and acoustic effects, such as the broad-spectrum hiss one hears in a kettle not yet heated to the point where bubbles boil to the surface.

Detailed version:

Backpack

[5] Boiling
Boiling is something we see every day and is very important in many jobs and industries. For example, we use boiling when we cook food, clean things by killing germs, separate liquids in distillation, and make chemicals. Boiling starts when the pressure of the vapor inside the liquid becomes the same or higher than the pressure around the liquid. This lets bubbles form inside the liquid. These bubbles get bigger and rise to the surface, which makes the liquid bubble and boil. When a liquid boils, it uses a special kind of heat called the latent heat of vaporization. This heat helps change the liquid into gas, but it does not make the temperature go up while boiling is happening.

[4] Boiling
Types > Transition: Transition boiling may be defined as the unstable boiling, which occurs at surface temperatures between the maximum attainable in nucleate and the minimum attainable in film boiling. The formation of bubbles in a heated liquid is a complex physical process which often involves cavitation and acoustic effects, such as the broad-spectrum hiss one hears in a kettle not yet heated to the point where bubbles boil to the surface.

[5] Boiling
Boiling is a bit more complicated than just bubbles rising in a pot. It involves how heat moves, how the liquid flows, and how bubbles start to form. There are different types of boiling. One type is called nucleate boiling, where tiny bubbles form on special spots on a hot surface.

units.question: Tell me how to cut and time garlic in a vegetable saute if I want the strongest garlic taste.
units.gold: Pungency is released by cutting, so the finer the cut the stronger: minced beats chopped, which beats sliced. Heat mellows the sharpness, and longer cooking makes garlic milder and sweeter as compounds break down. So mince it and add it near the end, about 30 seconds before the vegetables are done. Marinating ingredients with raw crushed garlic before a short cook also boosts the flavour.
rubric: States finer cutting releases more pungency
States cooking mellows garlic, longer is milder/sweeter
Recommends adding minced garlic about 30 seconds before the end
Penalize: advising to fry garlic first for a long time for maximum pungency

units.sources:
[1] Garlic bread
Garlic bread (also called garlic toast) consists of crusty bread slices topped with garlic and butter, and additional herbs such as oregano, chives or parsley. Garlic bread is typically made using a baguette, or sometimes ciabatta which is partially sliced downwards, allowing the condiments to soak into the loaf while keeping it in one piece. The bread is then stuffed through the cuts with oil and minced garlic before baking.

[2] Is wild garlic edible? How do you prepare it?
Answers > Answer (score 31, accepted): Here in Slovenia, the use of wild garlic is quite widespread. Although the whole plant, including bulbs, is edible, leaves are most commonly used.

I tried only leaves so far, so I can share my experience with only them.

Gathering

Young, light-green leaves are a bit more aromatic, but smaller; older are darker and larger. I pick a mix of both and look for undamaged, clean leaves. (I found very few with a bit chewed out by some animal; sometimes there are some webs on the bottom side, maybe spiders, not sure. It's no problem removing them, but if a leave is already "settled" I like to leave it intact.) I pick a leaf with the stem, somewhere at the middle.

Leaves of lily-of-the-valley are similar to wild garlic and are poisonous. To confirm that a leaf is wild garlic, I do the following:

[3] Is wild garlic edible? How do you prepare it?
Answers > Answer (score 31, accepted): - smell the leaf (must be like garlic),
- look at the underside of the leaf (a bit lighter than the top),
- each leaf grows from the ground on its own stem, whereas lily-of-the-valley grows several leaves from one stem (seen here),
- lily-of-the-valley has pronounced lines on the underside (also seen in the linked image above).

A good handful should be enough for one person for a risotto. I put it in a paper bag and it stores well several days in the fridge, but it's best used fresh to keep the most aroma.

Use

Wild garlic can be used raw in salads or more commonly to add flavor to soups, risottos, etc. It can be made into a pesto for later use.

Rinse leaves before use. Chop them to your liking and add them towards the end of your dish so it retains more flavor. You can also sauté it on olive oil or butter beforehand for a minute.

units.question: Explain why ice cream recipes warm the dairy first and then cook it again after the egg yolks go in.
units.gold: Warming the milk, cream and sugar first dissolves the sugar fully, avoiding a gritty custard. Adding some warm dairy to the beaten yolks tempers them, raising their temperature gradually so they do not scramble when the rest goes in. The final heating cooks the custard to about 155-160 F, the minimum for eggs, without going higher. Mixing everything cold and heating at once can work for small batches, but for large batches the stepwise method is faster and less likely to scorch.
rubric: Explains warming dairy and sugar dissolves the sugar (smooth texture)
Explains tempering prevents scrambled yolks
Gives the final cooking target around 155-160 F
Notes all-at-once can work for small batches but is impractical for large ones
Penalize: claiming the two steps are purely tradition with no effect
units.answer:
The passages found don't support this answer. From the model's memory, may be wrong:
Ice cream recipes warm the dairy first to ensure it is at the right temperature for cooking, then cook the egg yolks separately to achieve the desired consistency. The dairy is heated to a temperature where it can be blended with other ingredients, and the egg yolks are cooked separately to maintain their structure and texture. This method ensures the ice cream remains smooth and creamy. The dairy is often blended with sugar and cream, and the egg yolks are added after the dairy is warmed to avoid overcooking. This approach allows for a better balance of flavors and textures in the final product.

[4] Ice cream
Preparation: There are lots of ways to make ice cream. Most people don't make ice cream, because it is easier to buy.

Shops make ice cream by mixing cream and other things like milk, sugar, and eggs. Then they add flavoring (something that adds flavor to a food). Then they freeze it.

A method of making ice cream is by putting cream, milk, and sugar in a plastic bag. Then put ice and salt in a bigger bag. Putting the smaller bag inside the bigger bag, and then shaking it for five to 10 minutes will make ice cream.

[5] Scrambled eggs
Sample recipe: The eggs and a large piece of butter are put into a saucepan over a low heat. The egg whites and egg yolks are then "scrambled" or mixed together. The mixture should be mixed together all the time they are being cooked.

When cooked a little créme frâiche is added. This is because the eggs will be hot enough to carry on cooking themselves. Adding a cool liquid will stop the eggs from overcooking. Some salt and pepper or other seasoning can be added to taste as well.

In the home the eggs can be mixed together first and then poured into a pan. The créme frâiche does not need to be added if the eggs will be eaten almost immediately.

Properly made, the eggs should be moist and creamy consistency. If any liquid is coming from the eggs, it means the eggs have been overcooked or that the add the vegetables were undercooked.

units.question: Does a lender looking at my credit report lower my score?
units.gold: It depends on the type of inquiry. A hard pull, made with your permission when you apply for credit, lowers your score a little, typically a few points for a while. A soft pull, used for pre-approved offers, background checks such as renting, or checking your own report, has no effect. Several similar hard pulls within a short shopping window (for example mortgage shopping over a couple of weeks) count only once. Hard pulls matter mainly when you are about to apply for a mortgage.
rubric: Distinguishes hard pulls (lower score) from soft pulls (no effect)
States the drop from a hard pull is small and temporary
Notes rate-shopping inquiries within a short window count once
Gives examples of soft pulls (pre-approved offers, own checks)
Penalize: claiming every check of the file lowers the score
units.answer: A lender looking at your credit report may lower your score if they find negative information, such as late payments or defaults. This can affect your eligibility for loans or credit [3]. The credit report includes both public and private information, including your payment history [2]. A bad credit score can make it harder to get approved for credit or loans. The impact depends on the specific credit report and the lender's assessment.
units.sources:
[1] Credit rating
A credit rating is an evaluation of the credit risk of a prospective debtor (an individual, a business, company or a government). It is the practice of predicting or forecasting the ability of a supposed debtor to pay back the debt or default. The credit rating represents an evaluation from a credit rating agency of the qualitative and quantitative information for the prospective debtor, including information provided by the prospective debtor and other non-public information obtained by the credit rating agency's analysts. Credit reporting (or credit score) is a subset of credit rating.

[2] Credit history (cited)
Credit history or credit report is, in many countries, an information about past borrowing and repaying, including information about late payments and bankruptcy. The term "credit reputation" can be also used to describe credit history or credit score. In many countries, when a customer apply for credit from a bank, store or credit card company, their information is checked with credit monitoring organization. Such an organization will check if potential lender have history of some unpaid loans or other problems.

[3] Would a bad credit score affect your eligibility for US ESTA? (cited)
Answers > Answer (score 5): In this case we will be looking under inadmissibility due to criminal reasons. Mainly here we would be looking if you committed fraud which would in many cases be a Crime Involving Moral Turpitude (CIMT) that make you inadmissible if it doesn't qualify for the Petty Offense Exception under 212(a)(2)(A). To stretch this civil case into the realms of fraud is highly unlikely by any prosecutor considering the amount involved < $10k.

[4] Would a bad credit score affect your eligibility for US ESTA? (cited)
Answers > Answer (score 5): What would happen if I fail to pay?

Chances are that they will process you for court, obtain a judgment against you, and try to collect by means such as garnishment of wages if you do have employment in the USA. Of course it will hit your credit at some point (if you have a social security number) and your credit score will take a deep dive and graveyard spiral into the dumpster.

Would it affect me later on if I apply for a ESTA visa for a visit?

NO. Grounds of Inadmissibility per INA: ACT 212 - GENERAL CLASSES OF ALIENS INELIGIBLE TO RECEIVE VISAS AND INELIGIBLE FOR ADMISSION; WAIVERS OF INADMISSIBILLITY Sec. 212. [8 U.S.C. 1182] is what is used to determine your eligibility or otherwise for a visa/ESTA (immigration benefit).

units.question: I always settle my credit card statement the day it arrives instead of waiting for the due date. Am I losing anything?
units.gold: Very little. On a card with an interest-free grace period, paying early only forgoes the interest your cash could earn in savings until the due date; on a $2,000 monthly bill at 1% that is roughly $5 a year. One late payment would wipe out years of that gain through a late fee and interest, so paying early or setting autopay for the due date are both sensible. On a card with no interest-free period, paying sooner actually saves interest.
rubric: Explains the only cost is lost interest on cash during the grace period
Shows the amount is tiny (e.g. about $5/year on $2,000 at 1%)
Notes a single late fee outweighs the gain
Notes that without a grace period early payment saves interest
Penalize: claiming early payment hurts the credit score
units.answer:
The passages found don't support this answer. From the model's memory, may be wrong:
Setting your credit card statement early may help you catch errors or discrepancies sooner, but it doesn't necessarily prevent you from losing anything. If you pay early, you might avoid interest charges, but if you miss the due date, you could be charged late fees. Early payment can also help you manage your budget better. However, if you pay the statement day early, you may miss out on rewards or benefits that require payment by the due date.

units.question: To build credit, is it better to be added to a family member's premium card as an authorized user, or to open a secured card myself?
units.gold: Authorized-user status helps only if the issuer reports authorized users to the bureaus (not all do). If it does, your relative's on-time payments help you, but their missed payments or high utilisation can hurt you and you cannot control them. Your own secured card puts you in control and, if the issuer keeps the history when you upgrade to an unsecured card, builds length of credit. Being removed later can drop your score. The card's annual fee and perks do not affect the score.
rubric: Notes not all issuers report authorized users
Explains the relative's late payments or high utilisation can hurt you
Explains own card gives control and builds account history
States rewards or annual fee do not affect the score
Penalize: claiming a premium card's tier itself raises your score
units.answer:
Not found in this phone's offline library. From the model's memory, may be wrong:
Opening a secured card yourself may build credit more effectively, as it allows you to establish a positive credit history through regular payments. Being added as an authorized user on a family member's premium card can also help, but it may not build credit as directly. The best approach depends on your financial goals and the type of credit you want to build. Secured cards often require a deposit and can be a good starting point for credit-building.

units.question: Tell me how to get a refund check payable to me and my former roommate deposited when we now live in different cities.
units.gold: A check made out to both of you ("and") generally needs both endorsements, and a bank may refuse to deposit it into an account in only one name, so call the depositing bank first. Easier options: ask the landlord to reissue it as two checks for half each, or to make it payable "and/or"; or one of you endorses it "For Deposit Only", deposits it (an ATM deposit is less hassle) and pays the other their share separately.

units.sources:
[1] Seismic microzonation
Regional geology can have a large effect on the characteristics of ground motion. The site response of the ground motion may vary in different locations of the city according to the local geology. A seismic zonation map for a whole country may, therefore, be inadequate for detailed seismic hazard assessment of the cities. This necessitates the development of microzonation maps for big cities for detailed seismic hazard analysis. Microzonation maps can serve as a basis for evaluating site-specific risk analysis, which is essential for critical structures like nuclear power plants, subways, bridges, elevated highways, sky trains and dam sites. Seismic microzonation can be considered as the preliminary phase of earthquake risk mitigation studies. It requires multi-disciplinary contributions as well as comprehensive understanding of the effects of earthquake generated ground motions on man made structures. Many large cities around the world have put effort into developing microzonation maps for the better understanding of earthquake hazard within the cities.

[2] Seismic microzonation
Effect of site conditions on earthquake ground motion: It has long been recognized that the intensity of ground shaking during earthquakes and the associated damage to structures are significantly influenced by local geologic and soil conditions. Unconsolidated sediments are found to amplify ground motion during earthquakes and are hence more prone to earthquake damage than ground with hard strata. Modern cities built on soft sediments are especially vulnerable to damage caused by amplified ground motions.

units.question: Why do ordinary US bank transfers and direct deposits take a business day or more to clear?
units.gold: Because they run on the Automated Clearing House (ACH) network, which collects transactions during the day and settles them in a batch at the end of each business day. In the batch, banks net out what they owe each other, so instead of moving money for every individual payment, only the differences change hands, which turns many transactions into a few inter-bank transfers. If you need money moved faster, use a wire transfer, which costs an extra fee.
rubric: Names ACH and batch processing at the end of each business day
Explains netting: only the differences between banks move
Mentions wire transfer as the faster, paid alternative

units.question: What stops American credit unions from accepting any customer who walks in?
units.gold: Federal law. 12 USC 1759(b) limits credit union membership to groups sharing a common bond (an employer, an organisation, a community) or to people in a particular area, and each charter states who may join. Credit unions are member-owned, not-for-profit institutions with preferential tax and regulatory treatment; the limits exist so they do not compete too freely with banks, which oppose loosening them. Credit unions would like looser rules but not at the cost of their tax advantages.

Explains the limits offset their tax advantages so banks stay competitive
Penalize: claiming it is merely each credit union's marketing choice
units.answer:
The passages found don't support this answer. From the model's memory, may be wrong:
American credit unions are not restricted by any legal or regulatory barrier from accepting any customer who walks in. They operate like banks, and their policies are determined by their own board of directors. Credit unions often have specific membership criteria, but they are not prohibited from accepting new members. The primary factor is whether the customer meets the credit union's lending or service requirements.

units.question: I am moving a pre-tax 401(k) from an old job. Can it go into a Roth IRA, and which destination makes more sense?
units.gold: You can, but money moved from a pre-tax 401(k) into a Roth is taxed as a conversion. A common approach is to roll it into a traditional IRA first (no tax now) and then convert to Roth in chunks that fill your current tax bracket. Choose Roth if you expect a higher tax rate in retirement than now, traditional if lower. An IRA usually offers more investment choices and lower fees than a 401(k), though a 401(k) allows penalty-free withdrawals after separating at 55.

The choice depends on your expected tax situation and long-term financial goals.

[3] Transferring money from a non EU country to UK bank
Answers > Answer (score 1, accepted): To answer the tax question, from my understanding you need to declare any income (that isn't already declared by your employer). If that money doesn't come from an income (for example, you're using your savings or your family is helping you with money), you shouldn't need to declare it or pay tax from it. If you are making money from online freelancing and getting paid into your Moldovan bank account and then optionally moving money into your UK bank, you would likely need to declare this income as you are a tax resident in the UK and need to pay tax from any earnings you make. But the act of transferring money around on its own isn't considered an income. Obviously, you may attract some kind of attention from the transfer companies or the banks if you start moving huge sums of money around (due to the money laundering laws and hence financial companies and banks checking where the money comes from, which will 99.99% not happen to you if you are moving £1000 or less in a month). Either way Personal Finance & Money Stack Exchange is definitely a better place to answer this part of the question more appropriately.

units.question: Since 401(k) withdrawals are taxed as ordinary income rather than at the lower capital-gains rate, is a regular brokerage account the better deal?
units.gold: Usually not, because the comparison is not like for like. Money for a taxable account has already been taxed as income before you invest it, and then you also pay tax on dividends and capital gains. With a flat 20% rate, $10,000 in a traditional 401(k) growing tenfold leaves $80,000 after tax, the same as a Roth, while the taxable account nets less. Employer matching makes the 401(k) even better. Taxable accounts do win on liquidity and investment choice.

units.question: My high-deductible plan and HSA both started on January 1. Can I still put money in for the prior tax year before the April filing deadline?
units.gold: No. Prior-year contributions are allowed only if you were HSA-eligible (covered by a high-deductible plan) during that year. If your HDHP coverage started this January, your prorated limit for last year is zero and the last-month rule does not apply. Had you been covered last year and only opened the account late, you could contribute for that year until the April deadline. If you had an HDHP for part of last year, the limit is reduced proportionally.

units.question: Walk me through how vested restricted stock units are taxed, including what happens when I later sell the shares.
units.gold: RSUs are taxed as salary when they vest, on their value at that moment; brokers often sell part of the shares to cover the withholding. That vest-date value becomes your cost basis. From then on they are an ordinary stock position: selling within a year of vesting gives short-term gains, after more than a year long-term. Each vesting lot has its own date and basis, so you calculate gains per lot. Holding vested RSUs is economically like receiving cash and buying the stock.

units.answer:
The passages found don't support this answer. From the model's memory, may be wrong:
Vested restricted stock units (RSUs) are taxed based on the fair market value of the shares at the time of vesting. When you sell the shares, the gain is calculated based on the difference between the selling price and the fair market value at vesting. The tax treatment depends on whether the shares are classified as ordinary or capital gains. If the shares are held for more than a year, they may be taxed at the long-term capital gains rate. This applies to both the seller and the company, and the tax liability is determined by the IRS or the applicable tax authority.
units.sources:
[1] Joint-stock company
History: Finding the earliest joint-stock company is a matter of definition. Around 1250 in France at Toulouse, 96 shares of the Société des Moulins du Bazacle (Bazacle Milling Company) were traded at a value that depended on the profitability of the Society's mills. This was probably the first company of its kind in history.

The much more famous, wealthy and powerful English (later British) East India Company was granted an English Royal Charter by Elizabeth I on 31 December 1600. The Royal Charter gave the newly created Honourable East India Company a 15-year monopoly on all trade in the East Indies. The Company transformed from a commercial trading venture to one which ruled India.

[2] Joint-stock company
History: In 1602, the Dutch East India Company issued shares that were made tradable on the Amsterdam Stock Exchange. This invention helped joint-stock companies to attract capital from investors as they could now easily trade their shares. In 1612 it became the first 'corporation' in intercontinental trade with 'locked in' capital and limited liability.

[3] Capital gains tax
A capital gains tax is a tax on the profit realized on the sale of a non-inventory asset. The most common capital gains are seen from the sale of stocks, bonds, precious metals, real estate, and property.

Not all countries have a capital gains tax and most have different rates of taxation. Countries that do not impose a capital gains tax include Bahrain, Barbados, Belize, Cayman Islands, Isle of Man, Jamaica, New Zealand, Sri Lanka, Singapore, and others.

In some countries, such as New Zealand and Singapore, professional traders and those who trade frequently are taxed on such profits as a business income.

In the United Kingdom people paid £16.7 billion in capital gains tax in 2021-22.

units.question: In the UK, does earning a couple of pounds over the higher-rate threshold double my total income tax bill?
units.gold: No. UK income tax is marginal: the higher rate applies only to income above the threshold. In 2017/18 the first 11,500 pounds were tax free, income up to 45,000 was taxed at 20% and the next band at 40%, so earning 45,001 instead of 45,000 adds just 40p of tax. National Insurance also applies (12% up to the threshold, 2% above). One real trap: between about 100,000 and 120,000 the personal allowance is withdrawn, giving an effective 62% marginal rate.

Your tax liability is calculated based on your total income, and only the portion above the threshold is taxed at the higher rate. The threshold is £12,570 for the 2023–2024 tax year, and the higher rate is 22% on that amount. Your personal allowance and other factors also affect your tax bill.

units.question: When a target-date fund holds only other mutual funds, is its stated expense ratio charged on top of the underlying funds' ratios?
units.gold: Generally the fund passes the underlying costs through rather than adding a second full layer, but you must read the prospectus fee table. For the Vanguard target-date example, the prospectus shows a pass-through rather than an extra charge. In another case, a T. Rowe Price retirement fund charges no management fee itself but bears its pro-rata share of the acquired funds' expenses, which are listed under "acquired fund fees and expenses". So the total cost is the weighted underlying expenses plus any fee the fund itself charges.
rubric: Says the expense ratio usually reflects underlying fund costs (pass-through) rather than doubling

units.answer: Target-date funds typically do not charge an additional expense ratio on top of underlying mutual funds. Instead, their expense ratio is incorporated into the underlying funds' ratios. The expense ratio is applied to the total value of the fund. The fund's total expense ratio is calculated based on the underlying funds' ratios. The expense ratio is a percentage of the fund's net assets.

units.question: Explain whether a basket ETF rises when one of its stocks jumps 10%, even with nobody buying the ETF itself.
units.gold: Yes, the ETF price follows its holdings. Authorized participants can create or redeem ETF shares in exchange for the underlying stocks, so whenever the ETF price drifts from the value of its holdings they profit by arbitraging the gap, pushing the prices back in line. For ETFs with liquid holdings the deviation is tiny; for illiquid holdings such as emerging markets the ETF can trade at a noticeable premium or discount between trades of the holdings.

units.question: I got a $5,000 windfall and owe on a big card at 14%, a store card with deferred interest ending soon at 24%, and a few small zero-interest cards. Tell me how to split it.
units.gold: Pay off the deferred-interest store card first: if the full balance is not cleared by the promotion deadline, the interest for the whole period is charged retroactively. Then put the rest on the highest-rate debt (the 14% card); the usual rule is highest interest first, then larger balances, with low-interest debt last. Keep a small emergency fund so a surprise expense does not go back on a card. Keep paying more than the minimum, since a lower minimum only prolongs the debt.
rubric: Prioritises the deferred-interest card before the deadline
Explains deferred interest is charged for the whole period if not fully paid
Recommends paying highest interest rate next
Mentions an emergency fund and not dropping to minimum payments
Penalize: recommending paying the zero-interest cards first

[1] Best way to split costs during travelling
Answers > Answer (score 18): I've always used your option number 3. It's not difficult to figure out how much every one has paid!

Take a notebook with you in your trip. Draw 4 columns, the first one for item names you must pay in common (transport, accommodation...) and the other 3 columns for the amount each person paid for each item.

For example, if Person 1 pay $10 a taxi, you write in the first column "Taxi from A to B" and the amount 10 under the column for Person 1. If Person 1 and Person 2 pay $30 each one for a Hotel, you'll write "Hotel at X" and 30 under Person 1 and Person 2.

Item         |   Person 1   |  Person 2  |   Person 3
-----------------------------------------------------
Taxi A to B  |     10       |            |
Hotel at X   |     30       |    30      |

When you finish your trip, sum up the 3 columns. It will give you the amount paid for each people. Sum up these 3 values and divide by 3 (mean) and you have the balance each one has to pay to others.

[2] Best way to split costs during travelling
Answers > Answer (score 18): For example, Person 1 has a sum of 100, Person 2 has a sum of 120 and Person 3 has a sum of 80. The mean is (100 + 120 + 80) / 3 = 100. So Person 1 is ok because he/she has paid exactly the mean; Person 2 is 120 - 100 = 20 over the mean so he/she must get $20 from Person 3 that is 80 - 100 = -20, $20 under the mean.

Item         |   Person 1   |  Person 2  |   Person 3
-----------------------------------------------------
Taxi A to B  |     10       |            |
Hotel at X   |     30       |    30      |
 ........    |    ....      |   ....     |
-----------------------------------------------------
                  100            120           80
 Mean        |       (100 + 120 + 80) / 3 = 100
 Diff        |     0        |     20     |    -20

This way each person can pay with their own credit card and it's easy to know how much is the balance to pay each other.

units.question: I am 65 with large savings and a sales rep is pushing a whole life policy paying 1.7% that I would fund with $400k up front plus $75k a year. Is that wise?
units.gold: Probably not. Invested instead at a market return around 8%, the same contributions would grow to about $1.95 million in ten years against about $1.3 million in the policy, an opportunity cost of roughly $430k (still $178k at a conservative 5%). Equivalent term cover for a healthy 65-year-old costs far less, about $11,000 a year for $2 million over ten years. It also makes little sense to earn 1.7% while paying 3.5% on a mortgage; paying that down may remove the need for insurance.
rubric: Concludes the policy is a poor investment for this situation
Quantifies opportunity cost versus investing (hundreds of thousands)
Compares with much cheaper term life coverage
Notes earning 1.7% while paying a higher mortgage rate
Penalize: endorsing the policy mainly because payouts are tax free

You should consider consulting a financial advisor to evaluate the policy against your financial goals.
