units.question: List the cash I should have ready beyond a 20% down payment when buying my first home.
units.gold: Budget for: closing costs (from zero to about 2% of the mortgage); a good home inspection you commission yourself (about $500, possibly more than once if you look at several houses); property-tax escrow, which a bank may want a full quarter in advance; and a maintenance fund, for example $8-10k on a $100k house, since heating, water heater and appliances all fail eventually. A home warranty (about $250 a year) can cover early repairs. Keep the monthly payment a conservative share of take-home pay.
rubric: Mentions closing costs (up to about 2%)
Mentions a home inspection paid by the buyer
Mentions escrow of property tax in advance
Mentions a maintenance/repair reserve
Penalize: implying the down payment is the only cash needed
units.answer: You should have a down payment of at least 20% of the home's purchase price, and beyond that, you should have enough cash to cover closing costs, such as title insurance, attorney fees, and loan origination fees. Keep your cash in a concealed, safe location, like a money belt or first aid kit, to prevent theft [1]. Use a credit card or bank card for larger purchases to avoid carrying too much cash. If you're unsure, consult a financial advisor for personalized advice.
units.sources:
[1] Wikivoyage: Packing list (cited)
Buy > Payment methods: Segregating your methods of payment will protect you should you be robbed. The bulk of your cash and methods of payment should be stored in a concealed, safe location, such as a money belt tucked fully underneath your pants, or tucked away in your first aid kit, toiletry bag or in a hidden pocket in your baggage. Avoid having a bulge show where your currency is. Keep a credit card, ATM card or sufficient cash readily accessible, such as in a front pocket, which is closed by button or preferably with a zipper.

[2] Cash register
Cashiers and payment: Many modern cash registers and POS terminals also allow payments by electronic funds transfer (EFT), such as a debit card or credit card. In this case, the customer has to use a small machine next to the cash register or POS terminal that reads the data from his or her card. Many debit and credit cards now have a feature called contactless payment, which allows the user to simply tap his or her card on the reader to pay, making it quicker than other methods such as a chip or magnetic stripe. Companies like Apple, Google, and Microsoft have all made NFC-based mobile payment systems for platforms like iOS, Android, and Windows.

[3] Cash register
History and types: The person who invented the cash register was James Ritty, who came from Ohio and owned a bar in Dayton. In 1878, he found out that the people who worked in the bar kept on stealing money. When he noticed a part of a ship which counted how many times the propeller turned, he used the same idea to build a machine that could count different amount of sales. He got a patent on his machine and started a company the next year to make them, but it was not popular and the company, which became the National Cash Register Company in 1884, was sold to John H. Patterson.

[4] Cash register
History and types: Although the first cash registers were completely mechanical (they used moving parts such as gears and pulleys), and later ones were powered by electricity, today's cash registers use electronics. Computer chips are used to add up the prices of different items, show the total amount that has to be paid as well as the change that has to be given back to the customer, open the cash drawer after the customer has paid, and print a receipt as a proof of purchase.

[5] Answering how much money I have brought with me
Answers > Answer (score 4): When entering the US you need to declare cash or other monetary instruments exceeding a total of $10,000. You might be asked if you have over that amount, but it would not be typical to be asked how much money you have in general. As noted in comments, it is possible that you might be asked if you have sufficient funds to support yourself during your stay. In either case, if you were asked, I would politely say that you didn't bring any cash, and that you'll be using your bank card to support yourself.

[6] What should I put under Savings and Investments in the UK Visa application?
Answers > Answer (score 1): You should put your interest amount only. they are asking you about your income from your saving. do not put how much savings you have. kindly mention how much you get interest from your savings.so you should put 3 thousand pesos as per your details.

units.question: For someone who would pay cash and values convenience over savings, does leasing a car or buying it outright make more sense?
units.gold: Buying for cash usually wins on both counts. A lease is essentially renting: at the end you have no equity, and a lease is only cheaper if the payments are below the car's depreciation, which would mean the lessor loses money. Buying for cash is one transaction, while a lease means monthly payments plus a negotiation at turn-in or buyout every two or three years, so 3-5 negotiations over ten years. Leasing's advantage is mostly fewer repairs, since cars are new during the lease.
rubric: States a lease is essentially renting with no equity at the end
Explains a lease is only cheaper if payments are below depreciation
Notes buying for cash is a single transaction vs repeated lease negotiations
Mentions fewer repairs as the main convenience of leasing
Penalize: claiming leasing is cheaper for a cash buyer in general
units.answer:
The passages found don't support this answer. From the model's memory, may be wrong:
Leasing a car may be more convenient for someone who values convenience over savings, as it allows for lower upfront costs and flexibility in mileage. However, buying a car outright can provide better long-term value and ownership. The decision depends on factors like usage, budget, and long-term plans. Leasing may be better for short-term use, while buying is better for long-term ownership.

[1] Best way to physically move monetary value around
Answers > Answer (score 5): I would suggest cash. It's more voluminous but lighter than gold and certainly very liquid. In $100 bills (using this as an example because someone did the calculations for me but you could use EUR 500 or CHF 1000 to save some space and have more colorful luggage), it seems perfectly possible to carry $420k (the value of a Good Delivery gold bar) with you.

Sources:

- Computations for one million dollars
- Here is how it looks like

And with Swiss Francs, you can take even more (thanks @drat for the link!) as CHF 1 million (>$1 million) should only be a bit more than 1 kg and 1L in new CHF 1000 bills (and, like everything Swiss, the bills you get are often squeaky clean compared to small euro or dollar bills that circulate a lot). Swiss Francs might be slightly more difficult to use abroad but, amazingly, in Switzerland, you can easily pay your groceries (or a car…) with large bills and nobody would bat an eye.

[2] Best way to physically move monetary value around
Answers > Answer (score 5): One issue is that using cash might make a difference as far as cash control regulations are concerned. For example, European Union rules require you to declare that much money when leaving the EU but do not cover gold (some countries like the US or France do require gold, at least as bullion, to be declared as well so that's moot there).

That's a bit of extra hassle (and it might fail your “convenience” criterion) but since people who carry a lot of cash or gold around usually obtained it through legitimate means and obviously paid their taxes, it's not a big deal.

units.question: My bank looks financially shaky, but my balance is within the FDIC limit. Should I move my money out?
units.gold: If you truly believe it is failing, moving is reasonable, but with insured deposits there is little urgency. The FDIC is backstopped by the government (it can borrow from the Treasury), and when a bank fails another bank usually takes over its accounts with little or no interruption, perhaps a day without ATM access. The worst case is waiting about a week for a check from the FDIC. If being without that money for a few days would hurt you, move it.
rubric: Notes insured deposits are protected so urgency is low
Explains failing banks are usually taken over with little disruption
Mentions the worst case is a short wait (about a week) for FDIC payment
Advises moving if short-term illiquidity would be a problem
Penalize: claiming insured deposits are likely to be lost
units.answer:

However, if you're concerned about the bank's stability, moving funds could be a precaution. Consider consulting a financial advisor for personalized advice.

units.question: Explain why the Series I savings bond rate fell while the Federal Reserve was raising interest rates.
units.gold: I bond rates are not set by the Fed. The composite rate combines a fixed rate, set by the Treasury for the life of the bond, with a semiannual inflation rate based on recent CPI-U changes: composite = fixed + 2 x semiannual inflation + fixed x semiannual inflation. When measured inflation started falling, the I bond rate fell with it, even as the Fed raised rates to push future inflation down. The fixed part stayed at zero from 2020 to November 2022.
rubric: States the I bond rate follows measured inflation (CPI-U), not the Fed funds rate
Gives or describes the composite-rate formula (fixed + inflation component)
Explains the Fed raises rates to reduce future inflation while I bonds track past inflation
Penalize: claiming the Fed directly sets I bond rates
units.answer:
The passages found don't support this answer. From the model's memory, may be wrong:
The Series I savings bond rate fell as the Federal Reserve raised interest rates because the bond's yield is tied to the Fed's policy rate, and when rates increase, the bond's吸引力 decreases. The bond's interest rate is determined by the Fed's policy rate, so when the Fed raises rates, the bond's rate also rises, but the bond's maturity value is fixed. The bond's yield is calculated based on its face value and the time to maturity, so when the Fed raises rates, the bond's yield increases, but the bond's rate is not directly affected. The bond's rate is not directly tied to the Fed's policy rate, but it is influenced by the Fed's actions, leading to a decrease in the bond's rate as the Fed raises rates.

[1] Interest rate
In debt financing, companies borrow capital from a bank, in the expectation that the borrowed capital may be used to generate a return on investment greater than the interest rates. Failure of a borrower to continue paying interest is an example of default, which may be followed by bankruptcy proceedings. Collateral is sometimes given in the event of default. In monetary policy and macroeconomics, the term "interest rate" is often used as shorthand for a central bank's policy rate, such as the United States Federal Reserve's federal funds rate.

[2] Federal Reserve
Over the years, events such as the Great Depression in the 1930s and the Great Recession during the 2000s have led to the expansion of central bank's remit. Congress established three key objectives for monetary policy in the Federal Reserve Act: maximizing employment, stabilizing prices, and moderating long-term interest rates. The first two objectives are sometimes referred to as the Federal Reserve's dual mandate.

[3] 2008 financial crisis
Austrian school economists attributed the crisis primarily to the Federal Reserve's ("Fed") prolonged policy of artificially low interest rates, arguing this generated a credit bubble and widespread malinvestment, compounded by the moral hazard created by government-backed entities such as Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac.

[4] 1998 Russian financial crisis
Crisis and effects: On 17 August 1998, the Russian government devalued the ruble. They also defaulted on domestic debt and declared a
moratorium on payments to foreign creditors.
- the ruble/dollar trading band would expand from 5.3–7.1 RUR/USD to 6.0–9.5 RUR/USD;
- Russia's ruble-denominated debt would be restructured in a manner to be announced at a later date; and, to prevent mass Russian bank default,
- a temporary 90-day moratorium would be imposed on the payments of some bank obligations, including certain debts and forward currency contracts.

On 17 August 1998 the government declared in the Joint Statement of the Government of the Russian Federation and the Central Bank of the Russian Federation that the state securities (GKOs and OFZs), with due dates through 31 December 1999, would be changed into new securities. The terms of the GKO/OFZ restructuring were also determined in the following acts:

[5] 1998 Russian financial crisis
Crisis and effects: - Decree of the Government of the Russian Federation №1007 of 25 August 1998
- Decree of the President of the Russian Federation №888 of 25 August 1998
- Decree №1787-р of 12 December 1998 on novation of state securities
- Federal Law on Top-Priority Measures in the Field of Budget and Tax Policy

[6] Quantitative easing
History: The US Federal Reserve used policies similar to quantitative easing during the Great Depression of the 1930s.

[7] Great Recession
The causes of the Great Recession include a bunch of weak-points that developed in the finance system. Another cause is a series of events that began with the bursting of the United States housing bubble in 2005–2012. When housing prices fell and homeowners began to abandon their mortgages, the value of mortgage-backed securities held by investment banks went down in 2007–2008. This caused many banks to collapse or be bailed out in September 2008. This 2007–2008 phase was called the subprime mortgage crisis. The combination of banks unable to provide funds to businesses, and homeowners paying down debt rather than borrowing and spending, resulted in the Great Recession. It began in the U.S. officially in December 2007 and lasted until June 2009, lasting over 19 months.

- Russia's ruble-denominated debt would be restructured in a manner to be announced at a later date; and, to prevent mass Russian bank default,
- a temporary 90-day moratorium would be imposed on the payments of some bank obligations, including certain debts and forward currency contracts.

On 17 August 1998 the government declared in the Joint Statement of the Government of the Russian Federation and the Central Bank of the Russian Federation that the state securities (GKOs and OFZs), with due dates through 31 December 1999, would be changed into new securities. [5] 2008 financial crisis
Austrian school economists attributed the crisis primarily to the Federal Reserve's ("Fed") prolonged policy of artificially low interest rates, arguing this generated a credit bubble and widespread malinvestment, compounded by the moral hazard created by government-backed entities such as Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac.

[6] Federal Reserve
Over the years, events such as the Great Depression in the 1930s and the Great Recession during the 2000s have led to the expansion of central bank's remit. Congress established three key objectives for monetary policy in the Federal Reserve Act: maximizing employment, stabilizing prices, and moderating long-term interest rates. The first two objectives are sometimes referred to as the Federal Reserve's dual mandate.

[7] Interest rate
In debt financing, companies borrow capital from a bank, in the expectation that the borrowed capital may be used to generate a return on investment greater than the interest rates. Failure of a borrower to continue paying interest is an example of default, which may be followed by bankruptcy proceedings. Collateral is sometimes given in the event of default. In monetary policy and macroeconomics, the term "interest rate" is often used as shorthand for a central bank's policy rate, such as the United States Federal Reserve's federal funds rate.

units.question: How do I get from Chiang Mai to Pai, and what should I know about the road?
units.gold:
Most people go by **minivan** from Chiang Mai's Arcade Bus Terminal (Terminal 3) to Pai. The trip is about 135 km on Route 1095 and takes roughly 3 hours. The road is paved and generally in good shape, but it's known for its **762 curves**, and many people get motion sick.

**Ways to get there**
- **Minivan:** Operators like Prempracha leave about every hour from roughly 6:30 am to 5:30 pm. Fares are usually around ฿150–250 at the counter and more if you book online. Full-size buses don't run this route because the road is too narrow.
- **Private car or taxi:** Costs more, but you can stop whenever you need to. One-way car rentals are uncommon, so you'll usually have to return a rental car to Chiang Mai.
- **Motorbike:** Only a good idea if you're an experienced rider. Thailand requires foreigners to carry an International Driving Permit, and without the right licence your travel insurance may not cover a crash.

**About the road**
- **Motion sickness:** Take medication beforehand, eat lightly, sit near the front and look at the horizon. The halfway rest stop helps.
- **Condition:** Mostly well maintained, but there are some potholes and sandy patches.
- **Season:** November to February is the best time to go. In the May–October rainy season the road can be slippery, visibility can be poor, and landslides sometimes happen.
- **Safety:** There have been fatal minivan crashes on this road. One in November 2023 was caused by a tyre blowout on a curve at speed. Pick a reputable operator, wear a seatbelt, and ask the driver to slow down if needed. Travel in daylight.

Schedules and prices change, so check them before you go.
rubric: Minivan from Chiang Mai (Arcade terminal), about 3 hours (~135 km on Route 1095); also motorbike (novices: 5-6 h with stops)
Warns that the road is steep and winding with lots of curves (motion sickness; police report ~2 accidents/day on the Chiang Mai-Pai road)
No invented train line to Pai
units.answer: From Chiang Mai to Pai, you can take a bus or trek through Doi Inthanon National Park [2]. The road is scenic and well-maintained, but you should be prepared for some elevation gain and potential weather changes. The route is part of the Chiang Mai–Pai highway, and it's recommended to drive with a good vehicle and proper navigation. The journey takes about 4-5 hours, and you should check the latest road conditions before heading out.

Answers > Answer (score 3): From the North
Bus from Gällivare to Ritsem, there is a boat to Akkastugorna, where you can follow the first kilometers of Pajelantaleden to access Sarek from the north

From North-East
Bus from Gällivare to Ritsem, but exit at Suorva (probably have to ask the Bus driver for it) or Vietas. At Suorva you can cross the Suorvajaure on the artificial dam, at Vietas there is a boat. Once across the lake you can walk into Sarek from the North-East.

From the East
Bus from Gällivare to Ritsem, get out at Kebnats and take the boat over to Saltoluokta Fjällstation. There you'll find the Kungsleden and access to Sarek from the East. You can also continue Kunsleden to the south until you reach Akse, and then turn West into Sarek.

From the South
Bus from Murjek/Jokkmokk to Kvikkjokk, where you can follow the Kungsleden to the north, you can split of at many points towards Sarek (e.g. Partestugan, Partekietle) lying to the West of Kungsleden.

Both Gällivare and Murjek are reachable by train.

units.question: Which are the longest rivers on Earth, and why is the ranking of the top two disputed?
units.gold:
Most reference books list the **Nile (about 6,650 km)** as the longest river and the **Amazon (about 6,400 km)** as second. Some studies argue the Amazon is longer, so neither ranking is settled.

**Commonly cited top rivers (approximate lengths):**
1. Nile, Africa: about 6,650 km
2. Amazon, South America: about 6,400 km (some measurements give 6,800 km or more)
3. Yangtze, China: about 6,300 km
4. Mississippi–Missouri, USA: about 6,275 km
5. Yenisei–Angara, Russia/Mongolia: about 5,500 km
6. Yellow River (Huang He), China: about 5,460 km

The Ob–Irtysh, Paraná, Congo and Amur rivers usually come next. Exact figures differ from one source to another.

**Why the top two are disputed:**
A river's length depends on where you say it starts and ends, and there's no universal rule for either.
- **Where it starts:** The Amazon is usually traced to Apacheta Creek, at the head of the Apurímac River in Peru. A 2014 study argued the true source is on the Mantaro River, which gives a different length. The Nile's farthest source is also debated, between headstreams in Rwanda and Burundi.
- **Where it ends:** The Amazon reaches the Atlantic through a huge estuary around Marajó Island. A 2007 Brazilian survey ended its measurement on the island's southern side (Pará River). That added hundreds of kilometres and put the Amazon at about 6,800 km, roughly 105 km longer than the Nile. Ending at the northern channel takes that extra distance away.
- **Meanders and seasons:** Rivers wind, change course and flood, so the results also depend on map scale and measuring method.

So the Nile wins under the traditional definitions and the Amazon may win under others. Everyone agrees the Amazon is by far the largest river by the volume of water it carries.
rubric: Nile (~6,650 km) and Amazon (~6,400 km, or longer by some measurements) are the top two; Yangtze third
Explains the dispute: choice of source tributary and of the mouth/estuary changes the length
Does not name another river as the longest
units.answer:
The passages found don't support this answer. From the model's memory, may be wrong:
The longest rivers on Earth are the Nile and the Amazon. The ranking of the top two is disputed because the Nile is longer than the Amazon, but the Amazon is considered the longest in some sources due to its vast drainage basin. The dispute arises from different measurement criteria, such as total length or river system size. The Nile's length is widely accepted, but the Amazon's status is sometimes debated based on basin size.

[1] FIFA Women's World Ranking
Teams in the lead: From the beginning until 25 August 2023, the top spots in the women's rankings were held only by the United States and Germany. After the 2023 World Cup, Sweden is now at the top, Germany is ranked sixth, and the USA is ranked third. Before this, the United States and Germany were in the top two places most of the time, except for six times when Germany was third. The United States stayed in the top spot for the longest time, nearly 7 years, from March 2008 to December 2014.

[2] Gilgit-Baltistan
Gilgit Baltistan (), previously known as the Northern Areas, is the northern-most autonomous territory of Pakistan. In terms of land area it is bigger than Sierra Leone but smaller than Panama. It was part of the former Princely state of Kashmir and Jammu in 1800s and later leased to British eventually liberated after a planned liberation movement led by Gilgit Scouts.

It borders Azad Jammu and Kashmir in the south, Indian-administered Kashmir in the southeast, where the KPK province of Pakistan to the west, and internationally borders Afghanistan to the north. However, Tajikistan is separated by fourteen kilometers via Wakhan Corridor, the People's Republic of China to the northeast.

[3] Gilgit-Baltistan
Gilgit Baltistan, which became a single administrative unit in 1970, was formed from the amalgamation of the Gilgit Agency, the Baltistan District of the Ladakh Wazarat, and the states of Hunza and Nagar. Gilgit Baltistan remains part of the Kashmir dispute. The Government of Pakistan since 1947 Independence regards the entire area of Jammu and Kashmir as "Territory in dispute" to be resolved by a Plebiscite to be held throughout the former state to determine the area's final accession to either India, or the neighboring country of Pakistan. Gilgit Baltistan is governed by a governor and a chief minister, with the latter being elected by the legislative assembly. Gilgit Baltistan covers 72,971 km² (28,174 mi²) and is very mountainous. It had an estimated population of 1.8 million in 2015. Its capital city is Gilgit, and the largest city is Skardu. The region is home to five of the 14 eight-thousanders, including K2 ("National Mountain").
